title: Tobacco, vaping & alcohol: very brief advice
blurb: How tobacco and alcohol harm the mouth, Very Brief Advice (Ask, Advise, Act), smokeless tobacco and vaping, alcohol units and the AUDIT-C tool.
question: While updating a patient's medical history, he mentions he smokes 20 a day and 'enjoys a few pints most nights'. His gums look surprisingly pink and don't bleed, yet the dentist has found deep pockets. What advice should the team give, how do you deliver it in under a minute, and why might his gums look healthier than they are?

teach.h: Why the dental team gets involved
teach.body: Tobacco and alcohol are the two main risk factors for oral cancer, and using both together increases the risk far more than either alone. Smoking is also a major risk factor for periodontitis and tooth loss. Dental teams see many people who never visit a GP, often twice a year, so every appointment is a chance to help. DBOH asks the team to give Very Brief Advice at every opportunity, and dental nurses can deliver it as part of oral health advice.

teach.h: Very Brief Advice on smoking: the 3 As

letters.sub: Do you smoke? Record status: smoker, ex-smoker or never smoked
The best way to quit is support plus stop-smoking medicine
Refer to the local stop smoking service if they're interested

teach.caption: VBA takes about 30 seconds. You don't have to persuade anyone; you give the facts and offer help.

teach.h: What to say in each step
teach.body: Ask every patient whether they smoke and record the answer. Advise, without judging, that the most effective way to stop is a combination of behavioural support and medication, such as varenicline or a mix of short-acting and long-acting nicotine replacement therapy (NRT). Act on their response: refer those who want to quit to local stop smoking services. DBOH also notes that e-cigarettes may help some smokers to quit or cut down. Record the advice given.

teach.h: What tobacco does to the mouth
head: Effect
Why it matters
rows: More bone loss and tooth loss

teach.caption: Heavy tobacco staining at the gum margins, inflamed and receding gums, and a white patch on the lower lip. Any persistent white or red patch must be shown to the dentist.

teach.body: Smokeless tobacco, such as paan, gutkha and chewing tobacco, carries a high risk of oral cancer and is used in some communities. Ask about it using the names patients know locally; showing a picture can help. If used, explain the risks, give very brief advice and refer those who want to quit. E-cigarettes are far less harmful than smoking and can help smokers quit, but they are not risk-free and aren't advised for non-smokers or young people. Their long-term effects on the mouth are still being studied.

The UK Chief Medical Officers' low-risk guideline is not to drink more than 14 units a week on a regular basis, spread over three or more days, with some drink-free days. Pregnant women, or those who could become pregnant, are advised not to drink at all. Regularly drinking above 14 units raises the risk of oral cancer and other diseases. The team uses AUDIT-C, three questions about consumption, to assess risk and give brief advice.

teach.caption: Units = strength (% ABV) × volume (ml) ÷ 1,000. One unit is 10 ml of pure alcohol. Six pints of 4% lager is already about 14 units.

bands.label: Lower risk: positive feedback, keep it there
Increasing risk: brief advice to cut down
Higher risk: refer to GP or alcohol service

teach.text: Smoking reduces blood flow to the gums, so a smoker's gums may look pink and bleed less even with active periodontitis. Don't take a lack of bleeding as a sign of health in a smoker.

items: Tobacco and alcohol are the main oral cancer risks; together they multiply it.
VBA: Ask (record status), Advise (support + medication works best), Act (refer to stop smoking services).
Ask about smokeless tobacco by local names; e-cigarettes may help smokers quit but aren't risk-free.
Alcohol: no more than 14 units a week, spread over 3+ days; none in pregnancy.

summary: You can now explain how tobacco and alcohol damage oral health, deliver Very Brief Advice using Ask, Advise, Act, ask about smokeless tobacco and discuss vaping, calculate alcohol units and give the 14-unit guideline, and act on an AUDIT-C score.

A.q: What are the three steps of Very Brief Advice on smoking?
A.why: Very Brief Advice is Ask (and record), Advise (on the best way to quit) and Act (refer to support).

whyNot.2: These aren't the VBA steps; AUDIT-C is an alcohol tool.
whyNot.3: VBA doesn't include 'avoid'; the third step is to act on the patient's response.

A.q: What is the UK Chief Medical Officers' low-risk alcohol guideline?
options: No more than 21 units a week
No more than 7 units a week
No more than 14 units a day
No more than 14 units a week
A.why: The CMOs advise not drinking more than 14 units a week on a regular basis, spread over three or more days.

whyNot.0: 21 units was an old guideline for men; it was replaced by 14 for everyone.
whyNot.1: 7 units is lower than the guideline figure.
whyNot.2: 14 units is the weekly limit, not a daily one.

A.q: A smoker with periodontitis has pink gums that barely bleed on probing. What is the most likely explanation?
A.why: Smoking reduces blood flow to the gums, which can hide bleeding and redness even when disease is active.

whyNot.1: Deep pockets show disease is present despite the appearance.
whyNot.2: Lack of bleeding in a smoker doesn't mean the disease has stopped.
whyNot.3: Nicotine doesn't heal gums; smoking worsens periodontal disease.

B.q: A patient who smokes says they'd like to stop. Following VBA, what is the best action?
options: Refer to local stop smoking services
Give a leaflet and say no more
Suggest they cut down gradually alone
B.why: The Act step is to refer people who want to quit to local stop smoking support, where behavioural support and medicines are available.

whyNot.0: Telling someone to stop without support is far less effective.
whyNot.2: A leaflet alone doesn't act on their wish to quit.
whyNot.3: Going it alone is the least successful way to quit.

B.q: Roughly how many units are in a pint of 4% lager?

whyNot.0: 1 unit is a single 25 ml measure of 40% spirit.
whyNot.1: 1.5 units underestimates a pint of 4% lager.
whyNot.3: 4 units would be a much stronger or larger drink.

B.q: A patient's AUDIT-C score is 7. What does DBOH advise?
B.why: A score of 5 to 10 means increasing risk, so the team gives brief advice to encourage a reduction.

whyNot.0: Urgent hospital referral isn't indicated; 11+ is referred to a GP or alcohol service.
whyNot.1: A score of 7 shows risk, so advice should be given.
whyNot.2: Positive feedback alone is for scores of 4 or below.

C.q: Which combination increases the risk of oral cancer the most?
C.why: Tobacco and alcohol are the main oral cancer risk factors, and together they increase the risk much more than either alone.

whyNot.1: Fluoride protects teeth and is not a cancer risk factor.
whyNot.2: Sugar causes caries, not oral cancer.
whyNot.3: This isn't the combination DBOH highlights; tobacco plus alcohol is.

C.q: A patient chews paan daily. What is the best approach?
options: Ignore it, as it isn't smoking
Explain the risks and give VBA
Only mention it if a lump appears
C.why: Smokeless tobacco such as paan carries a high oral cancer risk, so the patient should be told the risks and given very brief advice.

whyNot.0: Smokeless tobacco is still harmful and strongly linked to oral cancer.
whyNot.2: Cigarettes are also very harmful; the aim is to stop tobacco use.
whyNot.3: Advice should be preventive, not wait for signs of cancer.

C.q: What does DBOH say about e-cigarettes?
options: They are as harmful as cigarettes
They should be banned in all patients
They may help some smokers quit
C.why: DBOH acknowledges that e-cigarettes may help some smokers quit or cut down.

whyNot.0: E-cigarettes are much less harmful than smoking, though not risk-free.
whyNot.1: DBOH doesn't advise banning them; they can help smokers quit.
whyNot.3: They are not advised for people who don't smoke.

reteach.title: Thirty seconds that could save a life
reteach.question: You're with a patient who smokes and you have half a minute. What exactly do you say?

blocks.body: Ask: 'Do you smoke at all?' Record the answer. Advise: 'The best way to stop is with support and stop-smoking medicine; that gives you the best chance of success.' Act: 'Would you like me to put you in touch with the local stop smoking service?' If they say yes, refer. If they say no, that's fine: note it and ask again next time. You aren't lecturing; you're opening a door.

blocks.caption: An ulcerated red and white patch on the side of the tongue, the kind of lesion linked to tobacco and alcohol. Any ulcer lasting more than 3 weeks needs urgent referral by the dentist.

explain.body: Ask and record smoking status. Advise that support plus medication is the most effective way to quit. Act by referring to local stop smoking services if they want help.

test.q: In VBA, what should the 'Advise' step tell a smoker?
options: Cutting down is as good as stopping
test.why: DBOH says to explain that behavioural support combined with medication, such as varenicline or combination NRT, is most effective.

whyNot.0: VBA gives clear health advice rather than leaving it at personal choice.
whyNot.2: Cutting down is not as beneficial as stopping.
whyNot.3: Quitting without support is the least successful method.

explain.body: Oral cancer, periodontitis, masked bleeding, slow healing and dry socket, implant failure, staining, bad breath and reduced taste. Smokeless tobacco also carries a high oral cancer risk.

explain.caption: Smoking speeds up the bone loss of periodontitis, while hiding the bleeding that would normally warn you.

test.q: Which of these is NOT a recognised effect of smoking on the mouth?
test.why: Smoking doesn't improve saliva's protection; it harms healing, gums and appearance.

whyNot.0: Smoking slows healing and raises the risk of dry socket.
whyNot.1: Smoking is a major risk factor for periodontitis.
whyNot.2: Tar staining is a common visible effect.

explain.body: Units = % ABV × ml ÷ 1,000. No more than 14 units a week, spread over 3 or more days. No alcohol in pregnancy.

test.q: How should someone who regularly drinks 14 units a week spread them, according to the CMOs?
test.why: The guideline advises spreading drinking evenly over three or more days rather than heavy single sessions.

whyNot.1: Drinking it all at once is binge drinking, which raises harm.
whyNot.2: Weekends only concentrates drinking into fewer days.
whyNot.3: This describes heavy drinking within a single session.

explain.body: Three consumption questions. 0–4: positive feedback. 5–10: brief advice to cut down. 11 or more: refer to the GP or a community alcohol service.

test.q: A patient's AUDIT-C score is 12. What is the appropriate action?
options: Refer to GP or alcohol service
test.why: A score of 11 or more indicates higher risk, so DBOH advises referral to the GP or a community specialist alcohol service.

whyNot.0: Positive feedback alone is for scores of 4 or below.
whyNot.1: Smoking advice is separate; this is an alcohol score.
whyNot.3: Waiting a year ignores a high-risk score.
